label: L18
title: Unconstrained minimization: gradient descent
brief:
Unconstrained minimization $\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} f(x)$ is the core problem of non-linear optimization, and its techniques carry over to constrained algorithms. A local minimum of a $C^2$ function must satisfy $
abla f(x^*)=0$ and $
abla^2 f(x^*)\succeq 0$, while $
abla f(x^*)=0$ with $
abla^2 f(x^*)\succ 0$ is sufficient; for a convex $f$ every stationary point is a global minimum, as in ridge regression where $ eta^*=(X^	op X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^	op y$. Descent methods move along directions with $
abla f(x^k)^	op d^k<0$; gradient descent takes $d^k=-
abla f(x^k)$ and produces monotonically decreasing objective values. For an $M$-smooth convex $f$ with constant step $\alpha\le 1/M$ it converges sub-linearly, $f(x^k)-z^*\le\|x^0-x^*\|^2/(2\alpha k)$, and adding $m$-strong convexity gives linear convergence with factor $1-m/M$. Speed in practice depends on the step-size rule (constant, diminishing, exact or backtracking line search), the starting point, and the conditioning of the Hessian, which diagonal scaling and norm-based steepest descent address.
kp: Local min of a $C^2$ $f$ $\Rightarrow$ $\nabla f(x^*)=0$ and $\nabla^2 f(x^*)\succeq 0$: necessary, not sufficient.
$\nabla f(x^*)=0$ and $\nabla^2 f(x^*)\succ 0$ $\Rightarrow$ local min; indefinite Hessian $\Rightarrow$ not a local min; PSD only $\Rightarrow$ undecided.
Convex differentiable $f$: $x^*$ is a global min iff $\nabla f(x^*)=0$.
Ridge: $\nabla^2 f=X^\top X+\lambda I\succ 0$, so $\beta^*=(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y$ is the global min.
Descent direction: $\nabla f(x^k)^\top d^k<0$; gradient descent uses $d^k=-\nabla f(x^k)$.
Order $p$ / rate $\beta$: linear ($a^k$), sub-linear ($1/k$), super-linear ($(1/k)^k$), quadratic ($a^{2^k}$).
Step size: small = slow, large = unstable; exact line search = fewer, costlier iterations; backtracking = cheaper, more iterations.
Ill-conditioning ($\kappa\gg1$) slows GD (Kantorovich factor $((\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1))^2$); diagonal scaling $x^{k+1}=x^k-\alpha_kD\nabla f(x^k)$ re-units the problem.

topics.x: A local minimum of a twice continuously differentiable $f$ must have zero gradient and a PSD Hessian; zero gradient plus a PD Hessian guarantees a local minimum. The PSD case is inconclusive, as $f=x_1^3+x_2^2$ at the origin shows.

For a differentiable convex function the first-order condition $f(x)\ge f(x^*)+\nabla f(x^*)^\top(x-x^*)$ turns any stationary point into a global minimum. Ridge regression is a convex quadratic with PD Hessian $X^\top X+\lambda I$, so its stationary point is the closed-form global solution; in non-convex problems finding global minima is very hard.

topics.n: Descent methods and rates of convergence
topics.x:
A generic descent method repeats: pick $d^k$ with $
abla f(x^k)^	op d^k<0$, pick $\alpha_k>0$, update $x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_kd^k$, until e.g. $\|
abla f(x^k)\|\le\eta$. Gradient descent sets $d^k=-
abla f(x^k)$. Speed is measured by the order $p$ and rate $ eta$ in $\lim|z_{k+1}-z^*|/|z_k-z^*|^p= eta$.

topics.n: Smoothness, strong convexity and GD guarantees
topics.x: $M$-smoothness (Lipschitz gradient) gives a quadratic upper bound and $m$-strong convexity a quadratic lower bound on $f$. With these, GD on a convex $M$-smooth $f$ converges sub-linearly, and on an $m$-strongly convex one linearly with factor $1-m/M$.

The gradient changes by at most $M$ per unit of distance, so the curvature of $f$ is capped at $M$. Geometrically, at every point $f$ sits under a parabola of curvature $M$ that touches it there. Minimising that parabola is exactly a gradient step of $1/M$, which is why $\alpha=1/M$ always decreases $f$.

$f$ curves upward at least as fast as $\frac m2\|x\|^2$: it lies above its tangent plane plus a bowl of curvature $m$. That floor rules out flat regions, gives a unique minimiser, and makes a small gradient a certificate of near-optimality. With smoothness, $f$ is sandwiched between two parabolas, and the ratio $M/m$ sets how fast gradient descent converges.

Each GD step moves every coefficient by $\alpha\sum_ix_{ij}(y_i-\hat y_i)$ and shrinks it by $\alpha\lambda\beta_j$. Because the loss is convex, GD reaches the global minimum (wine-price example: 46 samples, 7 features); the step size drives the speed.

Step-size rules: constant, diminishing ($\alpha_k\to0$, $\sum\alpha_k=\infty$), exact line search, and backtracking (Armijo) line search. Small steps are slow, large steps unstable. For non-convex $f$ the starting point decides which stationary point GD reaches, so multiple starts help.

The condition number $\kappa=\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}$ of the (Hessian) matrix controls GD speed; Kantorovich bounds the per-step contraction by $((\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1))^2$ for quadratics with exact line search. Diagonal scaling $D=SS^\top$ is GD on $g(y)=f(Sy)$, and steepest descent under different norms gives GD ($\ell_2$), scaled GD (quadratic norm) and coordinate descent ($\ell_1$).

cards.f: Necessary optimality conditions for a local minimum of a $C^2$ function.
cards.b:
$
abla f(x^*)=0$ (first order) and $
abla^2 f(x^*)\succeq 0$ (second order). Proof: $
abla f(x^*)^	op d\ge0$ for all $d$, applied to $\pm e_i$; then a second-order Taylor expansion gives $d^	op
abla^2f(x^*)d\ge0$.
cards.x: Necessary only: a PSD Hessian at a stationary point does not certify a minimum.

cards.f: Second-order sufficient condition for a local minimum.
cards.b:
If $
abla f(x^*)=0$ and $
abla^2 f(x^*)\succ 0$, then $x^*$ is a local minimum: by continuity the Hessian stays PD in a ball $B(x^*,ho)$, so the Taylor remainder $ rac12y^	op
abla^2f(x^*+z)y>0$ there.
cards.x: Strict PD is what makes it sufficient; PSD is not enough.

cards.f: Why is the origin not a local min of $f(x)=x_1^3+x_2^2$?
cards.b: $\nabla f(0)=0$ and $\nabla^2 f(0)=\mathrm{diag}(0,2)\succeq0$, so both necessary conditions hold, yet $f(-\varepsilon,0)=-\varepsilon^3<0=f(0)$.
cards.x: The standard counterexample to treating PSD as sufficient.

cards.b: $\nabla^2 f=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&4-6x_2\end{pmatrix}$. At $(4,0)$: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&4\end{pmatrix}\succ0$ $\Rightarrow$ local min. At $(3,1)$: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}$, det $=-3$ $\Rightarrow$ indefinite, not a local min.
cards.x: Both points are stationary; only the Hessian separates them.

cards.f: Global optimality for a differentiable convex function.
cards.b: $x^*$ is a global minimum iff $\nabla f(x^*)=0$. Proof: convexity gives $f(x)\ge f(x^*)+\nabla f(x^*)^\top(x-x^*)=f(x^*)$ for all $x$.
cards.x: Convexity turns the local first-order test into a global certificate.

cards.f: Ridge regression: gradient, Hessian and optimal $\beta$.
cards.b: $f(\beta)=\frac12\|y-X\beta\|^2+\frac\lambda2\|\beta\|^2$; $\nabla f=-X^\top(y-X\beta)+\lambda\beta$; $\nabla^2 f=X^\top X+\lambda I\succ0$ since $u^\top(X^\top X+\lambda I)u=\|Xu\|^2+\lambda\|u\|^2>0$; $\beta^*=(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y$.
cards.x: $\lambda>0$ makes the Hessian PD even when $X^\top X$ is singular.

cards.f: At a stationary point, what does each Hessian case tell you?
cards.b: $\succ0$: local minimum. $\succeq0$: can be a local minimum (undecided). Indefinite: not a local minimum. If $f$ is convex, any stationary point is global.
cards.x: In non-convex problems, identifying global minima is very hard.

cards.f: Generic descent method: the direction condition and why $f$ decreases.
cards.b: Choose $d^k$ with $\nabla f(x^k)^\top d^k<0$ and $\alpha_k>0$, set $x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_kd^k$. To first order $f(x^{k+1})\approx f(x^k)+\alpha_k\nabla f(x^k)^\top d^k<f(x^k)$ when $\alpha_k$ is small enough.
cards.x: Stop when e.g. $\|\nabla f(x^k)\|\le\eta$; the method seeks a stationary point, not a certified minimum.

cards.f: Order $p$ and rate $\beta$ of convergence, with the four standard cases.
cards.b: $\lim_k |z_{k+1}-z^*|/|z_k-z^*|^p=\beta$. Linear: $p=1$, $0<\beta<1$ ($a^k$). Sub-linear: $p=1$, $\beta=1$ ($1/k$). Super-linear: $p=1$, $\beta=0$ ($(1/k)^k$). Quadratic: $p=2$ ($a^{2^k}$).
cards.x: Sub-linear and linear share $p=1$; the rate $\beta$ tells them apart.

cards.f: Define $M$-smooth and $m$-strongly convex, and the quadratic bounds each implies.
cards.b:
$M$-smooth: $\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|\le M\|x-y\|$, so $f(y)\le f(x)+
abla f(x)^	op(y-x)+ rac M2\|y-x\|^2$. $m$-strongly convex: $f(x)- rac m2\|x\|^2$ convex, so $f(y)\ge f(x)+
abla f(x)^	op(y-x)+ rac m2\|y-x\|^2$.
cards.x: $M$ caps curvature from above, $m$ guarantees it from below.

cards.f: GD convergence for $M$-smooth convex $f$, constant step $\alpha\le1/M$.
cards.b: $f(x^k)-z^*\le\frac{1}{2\alpha k}\|x^0-x^*\|^2$: sub-linear, $O(1/k)$. Within $\varepsilon$ after at most $\|x^0-x^*\|^2/(2\alpha\varepsilon)$ iterations.
cards.x: Worse start, smaller $\alpha$ or tighter $\varepsilon$ all mean more iterations.

cards.f: GD convergence for $M$-smooth, $m$-strongly convex $f$ with $\alpha=1/M$.
cards.b: $f(x^k)-z^*\le(1-\frac mM)^k(f(x^0)-z^*)$: linear with $c=1-m/M$; $O(\frac Mm\log\frac1\varepsilon)$ iterations. Proof: smoothness gives $f(x^{k+1})\le f(x^k)-\frac1{2M}\|\nabla f(x^k)\|^2$, strong convexity gives $z^*\ge f(x^k)-\frac1{2m}\|\nabla f(x^k)\|^2$.
cards.x: $M/m$ acts like a condition number: the closer to 1, the faster.

cards.f: GD update for one ridge-regression coefficient and its interpretation.
cards.b: $\beta_j^{k+1}\leftarrow\beta_j^k+\alpha\sum_i x_{ij}(y_i-\sum_l x_{il}\beta_l^k)-\alpha\lambda\beta_j^k$. If a prediction is below its target and $x_{ij}>0$, $\beta_j$ increases; the $\lambda$ term penalizes any growth.
cards.x: Iterative model adjustment driven by residuals, shrunk by the regularizer.

cards.f: Backtracking line search: the procedure.
cards.b: Start with $\alpha=s$. Accept if $f(x^k+\alpha d^k)\le f(x^k)+\sigma\alpha\nabla f(x^k)^\top d^k$ with $0<\sigma\le\frac12$; otherwise set $\alpha\leftarrow\beta\alpha$, $0<\beta<1$. Result: $\alpha_k=s\beta^{m_k}$.
cards.x: Exact line search: fewer iterations, more work each; backtracking: cheaper iterations, more of them.

cards.f: Condition number and the Kantorovich bound for quadratics.
cards.b: $\kappa(Q)=\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\ge1$. For $f=\frac12x^\top Qx-c^\top x+b$, $Q\succ0$, GD with exact line search: $f(x^{k+1})-z^*\le\left(\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}\right)^2(f(x^k)-z^*)$.
cards.x: $\kappa\approx1$: fast; $\kappa\gg1$: slow zig-zag. Beyond quadratics, $\kappa(\nabla^2f(x^*))\lesssim M/m$.

cards.f: Diagonal scaling and norm-based steepest descent.
cards.x: Example: $D=\mathrm{diag}(1/1000,1)$ cut $\kappa$ from 1,668 to 4.4 and iterations from 68 to 20.

cards.f: Intuition: what does $M$-smoothness say about $f$?
cards.b: The gradient changes by at most $M$ per unit of distance, so curvature is capped at $M$. At every point $f$ sits under a parabola of curvature $M$ that touches it there.
cards.x: A ceiling, not a floor: $\sin x$ is 1-smooth and not convex.

cards.f: Why is $\alpha=1/M$ the natural step for an $M$-smooth $f$?
cards.b: It minimises the quadratic upper bound at $x^k$: $x^{k+1}=x^k-\frac1M\nabla f(x^k)$ guarantees $f(x^{k+1})\le f(x^k)-\frac1{2M}\|\nabla f(x^k)\|^2$.
cards.x: On $\frac M2x^2$, any $\alpha>2/M$ diverges.

cards.f: Intuition: what does $m$-strong convexity say about $f$?
cards.b: $f$ curves up at least as fast as $\frac m2\|x\|^2$: it lies above its tangent plane plus a bowl of curvature $m$. No flat stretches, so the minimiser exists and is unique.
cards.x: Strictly convex is not strongly convex: $e^x$ flattens out to the left.

cards.f: The gradient as an optimality certificate under strong convexity
cards.b: $f(x)-z^*\le\frac1{2m}\|\nabla f(x)\|^2$: a small gradient proves near-optimality, because a bowl of curvature $\ge m$ cannot be flat far from its bottom.
cards.x: Fails for plain convexity: $x^4$ is so flat at the bottom that its gap $x^4$ dwarfs its squared slope $16x^6$.

cards.f: The parabola sandwich and the rate it gives
cards.b:
$f(x)+
abla f^	op(y-x)+ rac m2\|y-x\|^2\le f(y)\le f(x)+
abla f^	op(y-x)+ rac M2\|y-x\|^2$. Upper bound: each step drops $f$ by $ rac1{2M}\|
abla f\|^2$. Lower bound: $\|
abla f\|^2\ge2m(f-z^*)$. Together: $f(x^{k+1})-z^*\le(1- rac mM)(f(x^k)-z^*)$.
cards.x: $m\le M$ always; $M/m$ is the condition number that sets the speed.

cards.f: Hessian test for $M$ and $m$ (twice-differentiable $f$)
cards.b: $M$-smooth: all Hessian eigenvalues lie in $[-M,M]$. $m$-strongly convex: all eigenvalues are at least $m$, i.e. $\nabla^2f\succeq mI$. For a quadratic $\frac12x^\top Qx$: $M=\lambda_{\max}(Q)$, $m=\lambda_{\min}(Q)$.
cards.x: Standard fact, beyond the slides. Ridge: $m\ge\lambda$, $M=\lambda_{\max}(X^\top X)+\lambda$.

quiz.q: $x^*$ is a local minimum of a twice continuously differentiable $f$. Which must hold?
o: $\nabla f(x^*)=0$ and $\nabla^2 f(x^*)\succeq0$
$\nabla f(x^*)=0$ and $\nabla^2 f(x^*)\succ0$
$\nabla^2 f(x^*)\succ0$ only
$\nabla f(x^*)=0$ and $f$ convex
quiz.e: The necessary conditions are a zero gradient and a PSD Hessian. A PD Hessian is the sufficient condition; a local minimum can have a singular Hessian (the $f'=0$, $f''=0$ case).

quiz.q: For $f(x)=\frac12x_1^2+x_1x_2+2x_2^2-4x_1-4x_2-x_2^3$, what is $\nabla^2 f$ at the stationary point $(3,1)$ and what does it imply?
o: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}$, indefinite: not a local minimum
$\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&4\end{pmatrix}$, PD: local minimum
$\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}$, negative definite: local maximum
$\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}$, PSD: possibly a local minimum
quiz.e: $\partial^2f/\partial x_2^2=4-6x_2=-2$; det $=1\cdot(-2)-1=-3<0$, so the eigenvalues have opposite signs. It cannot be negative definite because the $(1,1)$ entry is $+1$.

quiz.q: For $f(x)=x_1^3+x_2^2$ at $x=0$, which statement is correct?
o: Both second-order necessary conditions hold, but $0$ is not a local minimum
$0$ is a local minimum because $\nabla^2 f(0)\succeq0$
$0$ fails the first-order condition
$0$ is a strict local maximum
quiz.e: $\nabla f(0)=(0,0)$ and $\nabla^2f(0)=\mathrm{diag}(0,2)\succeq0$, but $f(-\varepsilon,0)=-\varepsilon^3<0$. PSD at a stationary point is necessary, not sufficient.

quiz.q: $f$ is continuously differentiable and convex, and $\nabla f(x^*)=0$. What can you conclude?
o: $x^*$ is a global minimum
$x^*$ is a local minimum that may not be global
Nothing until you check $\nabla^2f(x^*)\succ0$
$x^*$ is a saddle point unless $f$ is strictly convex
quiz.e: Convexity gives $f(x)\ge f(x^*)+\nabla f(x^*)^\top(x-x^*)=f(x^*)$ for all $x$. No second-order check is needed; strict convexity would only add uniqueness.

quiz.q: Ridge regression with one feature: $x=(1,2)^\top$, $y=(1,2)^\top$, $\lambda=5$, objective $\frac12\|y-X\beta\|^2+\frac\lambda2\beta^2$. What is $\beta^*$?
quiz.e: $\beta^*=(X^\top X+\lambda)^{-1}X^\top y=5/(5+5)=0.5$. $\beta=1$ is the unregularized least-squares fit, which ignores $\lambda$.

quiz.q: In a generic descent method, $d^k$ is a valid descent direction at $x^k$ when:
o: $\nabla f(x^k)^\top d^k<0$
$\nabla f(x^k)^\top d^k>0$
$d^k$ is orthogonal to $\nabla f(x^k)$
quiz.e: A negative directional derivative makes $f(x^k+\alpha d^k)<f(x^k)$ for small $\alpha$. An orthogonal direction has zero first-order change, so no guaranteed decrease.

quiz.q: The sequence $z_k=1/k\to0$ converges with:
o: Order $p=1$, rate $\beta=1$: sub-linear
Order $p=1$, rate $\beta=1/2$: linear
Order $p=1$, rate $\beta=0$: super-linear
Order $p=2$: quadratic
quiz.e: $|z_{k+1}|/|z_k|=k/(k+1)\to1$, so $\beta=1$: sub-linear. Linear convergence needs the ratio to settle strictly below 1, as for $a^k$.

quiz.q: Which sequence (with $0<a<1$) converges quadratically?
o: $z_k=a^k$
quiz.e: $z_{k+1}/z_k^2=a^{2^{k+1}}/a^{2^{k+1}}=1$, so $p=2$. $(1/k)^k$ is super-linear: ratio $\to0$ with $p=1$, but not order 2.

quiz.q: Gradient descent on an $M$-smooth convex $f$ with $M=4$, step $\alpha=1/M$, and $\|x^0-x^*\|^2=8$. How many iterations does the lecture's bound need for $f(x^k)-z^*\le0.01$?
quiz.e: $k\ge\|x^0-x^*\|^2/(2\alpha\varepsilon)=8/(2\cdot0.25\cdot0.01)=1{,}600$. Using $\alpha=1$ instead of $1/4$ gives 400; the bound grows as $1/\varepsilon$, not $\log(1/\varepsilon)$.

quiz.q: $f$ is $M$-smooth and $m$-strongly convex with $M=10$, $m=1$; GD uses $\alpha=1/M$ and $f(x^0)-z^*=100$. The guaranteed bound on $f(x^2)-z^*$ is:
quiz.e: $c=1-m/M=0.9$, so $f(x^2)-z^*\le0.9^2\cdot100=81$. 90 is the one-step bound; 1 would use $c=m/M$.

quiz.q: Which summary of gradient-descent guarantees matches the lecture?
o: Convex + $M$-smooth: sub-linear; adding $m$-strong convexity: linear with $c=1-m/M$
Convex + $M$-smooth: linear; strongly convex: quadratic
Both cases converge quadratically with a constant step
Strongly convex: sub-linear with $c=m/M$
quiz.e: The bounds are $O(1/k)$ under convexity and $(1-m/M)^k$ under strong convexity. Quadratic convergence is not claimed for gradient descent.

quiz.q: A function $f$ is $m$-strongly convex if:
o: $f(x)-\frac m2\|x\|^2$ is convex
$\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le m\|x-y\|$
$f(x)+\frac m2\|x\|^2$ is convex
$f(y)\le f(x)+\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)+\frac m2\|y-x\|^2$
quiz.e: Strong convexity means convexity survives subtracting a quadratic. The Lipschitz-gradient condition and the quadratic upper bound describe $M$-smoothness instead.

quiz.q: In the GD update for ridge coefficient $\beta_j$, observation $i$ has $x_{ij}>0$ and prediction below its target. Its effect on $\beta_j$ is:
o: $\alpha x_{ij}(y_i-\hat y_i)>0$ pushes $\beta_j$ up, while $-\alpha\lambda\beta_j$ shrinks it
It pushes $\beta_j$ down, since residuals enter with a minus sign
None, because only the $\lambda$ term changes $\beta_j$
It pushes $\beta_j$ up, and $\lambda$ amplifies the increase
quiz.e: The update adds $\alpha\sum_ix_{ij}(y_i-\hat y_i)$ and subtracts $\alpha\lambda\beta_j^k$. A positive residual with positive feature raises $\beta_j$; the regularizer penalizes any increase.

quiz.q: What is the core trade-off in choosing a constant step size?
o: Too small: slow progress per iteration; too large: unstable behavior
Larger is always faster
Smaller always finds the global minimum
Step size only matters for non-convex $f$
quiz.e: The lecture shows slow convergence with small steps and instability with large ones, with faster convergence in between. A small step does not rescue a non-convex problem from local minima.

quiz.q: You run gradient descent on a non-convex $f$. What does the lecture recommend?
o: Run from several starting points in parallel and keep the best output
Use one start point; GD always finds the global minimum
Use a diminishing step size to guarantee a global minimum
Increase the tolerance $\eta$ until the result stops changing
quiz.e: GD finds a stationary point that depends on the initialization; multistart keeps the best. No step-size rule guarantees a global minimum without convexity.

quiz.q: Backtracking on $f(x)=x^2$ at $x^k=1$ with $d^k=-\nabla f(x^k)=-2$, $s=1$, $\beta=0.5$, $\sigma=0.5$. Which step is returned?
o: $\alpha=0.5$
$\alpha=1$
quiz.e: Test $f(1-2\alpha)\le1-4\sigma\alpha=1-2\alpha$. $\alpha=1$: $1\le-1$ fails. $\alpha=0.5$: $0\le0$ holds, so stop. Smaller steps also pass but are never tried.

quiz.q: For a quadratic with $\kappa(Q)=3$ and exact line search, Kantorovich bounds the per-iteration contraction of $f(x^k)-z^*$ by:
quiz.e: $((\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1))^2=(2/4)^2=0.25$. Forgetting the square gives 0.5.

quiz.q: Scaled gradient descent $x^{k+1}=x^k-\alpha_kD\nabla f(x^k)$ with $D=SS^\top\succ0$ is equivalent to:
o: Plain GD on $g(y)=f(Sy)$, a change of coordinates
Coordinate descent, one variable at a time
GD with a diminishing step size
Exact line search along $-\nabla f$
quiz.e: GD on $g$ gives $Sy^{k+1}=Sy^k-\alpha_kSS^\top\nabla f(Sy^k)$, i.e. the scaled update. Coordinate descent is steepest descent under the $\ell_1$ norm, a different rule.

quiz.q: In words, what does it mean for $f$ to be $M$-smooth?
o: Its gradient cannot change faster than $M$ per unit of distance, so its curvature is capped at $M$
$f$ grows at least quadratically away from its minimiser, with curvature at least $M$
$f$ itself changes by at most $M$ per unit of distance: $|f(x)-f(y)|\le M\|x-y\|$
$f(x)\le M$ for every $x$
quiz.e: Smoothness is Lipschitz continuity of the gradient, $\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le M\|x-y\|$: the slope can only turn so fast, so $f$ can never bend more sharply than curvature $M$. The tempting wrong answer, Lipschitz $f$, bounds the slope itself, not how fast the slope changes; and a curvature floor is strong convexity, the opposite bound.

quiz.q: Geometrically, the inequality $f(y)\le f(x)+\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)+\frac M2\|y-x\|^2$ says that, at every point $x$:
o: $f$ lies below an upward parabola of curvature $M$ that touches $f$ at $x$
$f$ lies above its tangent plane at $x$
$f$ lies above an upward parabola of curvature $M$ that touches $f$ at $x$
$f$ lies below its tangent plane at $x$
quiz.e: The right-hand side is the tangent plane plus a bowl $\frac M2\|y-x\|^2$, equal to $f(x)$ at $y=x$. Smoothness puts a ceiling over $f$. Lying above the tangent plane is plain convexity, and lying above a parabola is strong convexity: both are lower bounds, not this upper bound.

quiz.q: Why is $\alpha=1/M$ the natural step size for an $M$-smooth function?
o: Minimising the quadratic upper bound at $x^k$ over $y$ gives $y=x^k-\frac1M\nabla f(x^k)$: the step jumps to the bottom of the ceiling, so $f$ is guaranteed to drop
It is the step exact line search would choose at every iteration
It makes gradient descent reach $x^*$ in one iteration for any $M$-smooth $f$
It is the largest step for which $f$ stays convex along the search direction
quiz.e:
Setting the gradient of $f(x^k)+
abla f(x^k)^	op(y-x^k)+ rac M2\|y-x^k\|^2$ to zero gives $y=x^k-
abla f(x^k)/M$. Since $f$ is below this model and the model is minimised there, $f(x^{k+1})\le f(x^k)- rac1{2M}\|
abla f(x^k)\|^2$. Exact line search minimises $f$ itself, not the model, and generally picks a different step.

quiz.q: With $\alpha=1/M$ on an $M$-smooth $f$, each gradient step is guaranteed to decrease $f$ by at least:
o: $\frac1{2M}\|\nabla f(x^k)\|^2$
$\frac1M\|\nabla f(x^k)\|^2$
$\frac M2\|\nabla f(x^k)\|^2$
$\frac1{2M}\|\nabla f(x^k)\|$
quiz.e:
Plug $x^{k+1}-x^k=- rac1M
abla f(x^k)$ into the upper bound: $f(x^k)- rac1M\|
abla f\|^2+ rac M2\cdot rac1{M^2}\|
abla f\|^2=f(x^k)- rac1{2M}\|
abla f\|^2$. Forgetting the $+ rac M2\|\cdot\|^2$ penalty gives $ rac1M$; the decrease is in the squared gradient norm, not the norm.

quiz.q: For $f(x)=3x_1^2+x_2^2$, what is the smallest $M$ for which $f$ is $M$-smooth?
quiz.e:
$
abla f(x)=(6x_1,\,2x_2)$, so $\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|\le 6\|x-y\|$, with equality along $x_1$. For a twice-differentiable $f$, $M$ is the largest Hessian eigenvalue in absolute value; here $
abla^2f=\mathrm{diag}(6,2)$. Reading off the coefficient 3 forgets that $ rac{d^2}{dx^2}3x^2=6$; 8 adds the eigenvalues. (The Hessian test is standard, not stated on the slides.)

quiz.q: Which function on $\mathbb R$ is NOT $M$-smooth for any finite $M$?
quiz.e: $f'(x)=4x^3$ turns ever faster: $f''(x)=12x^2$ is unbounded, so no single $M$ caps the curvature. The others have bounded second derivatives: 2, at most $\frac14$ (the logistic $\sigma(1-\sigma)$), and at most 1.

quiz.q: $f(x)=\sin x$ on $\mathbb R$ is:
o: 1-smooth but not convex, so smoothness alone says nothing about global minima
not smooth, because smoothness requires convexity
convex and 1-smooth
1-strongly convex
quiz.e: $|\cos x-\cos y|\le|x-y|$, so the gradient is 1-Lipschitz, yet $\sin$ is not convex. Smoothness is only a ceiling on curvature; it controls how far a step can go wrong, not whether a stationary point is a global minimum. That needs convexity.

quiz.q: On $f(x)=\frac M2x^2$, gradient descent with constant step $\alpha$ gives $x^{k+1}=(1-\alpha M)x^k$. What happens with $\alpha>2/M$?
o: $|1-\alpha M|>1$: each step overshoots further than the last and the iterates diverge
It still converges, because $f$ is convex
It converges, but only sub-linearly
It converges in one step, because the step is large
quiz.e: Steps up to $1/M$ move monotonically toward 0; between $1/M$ and $2/M$ they overshoot but shrink; beyond $2/M$ the factor exceeds 1 in absolute value and the iterates blow up. Convexity does not save a step that is too long for the curvature: that is the "not too large" half of the step-size trade-off, and $1/M$ sits safely inside the stable range.

quiz.q: In words, what does it mean for $f$ to be $m$-strongly convex?
o: $f$ curves upward at least as much as $\frac m2\|x\|^2$ everywhere: a bowl with curvature at least $m$
Its gradient changes by at most $m$ per unit of distance
$f(x)\ge m$ for every $x$
$f$ is convex and has a global minimum
quiz.e: The definition, $f(x)-\frac m2\|x\|^2$ convex, says that after removing a bowl of curvature $m$ what is left still curves up, so $f$ has at least curvature $m$ in every direction. A gradient that changes by at most $m$ is smoothness (a ceiling, not a floor), and a convex function with a minimum can still be flat.

quiz.q: The inequality $f(y)\ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)+\frac m2\|y-x\|^2$ says that $f$ lies:
o: above its tangent plane plus a bowl of curvature $m$, so it pulls away from every tangent plane at least quadratically
above its tangent plane, and nothing more
below a parabola of curvature $m$ touching it at $x$
above a parabola of curvature $M$ touching it at $x$
quiz.e: Plain convexity gives only the tangent-plane bound; strong convexity adds $\frac m2\|y-x\|^2$, a quadratic floor. Lying below a parabola is smoothness, the matching ceiling with $M$.

quiz.q: Which convex function on $\mathbb R$ is NOT strongly convex for any $m>0$?
o: $f(x)=e^x$
$f(x)=\frac12x^2+3x$
quiz.e: $f''(x)=e^x$ is positive but tends to 0 as $x\to-\infty$, so no fixed $m>0$ works: far to the left $e^x$ is almost flat, and it has no minimiser at all. The others have curvature at least 2, 2 and 1. Strictly convex is not the same as strongly convex.

quiz.q: Why does strong convexity guarantee a unique global minimiser, when plain convexity does not?
o: The quadratic floor makes $f$ grow without bound in every direction and rules out flat stretches, so a minimiser exists and no two points can tie at the bottom
Every convex function already has a unique minimiser; strong convexity only speeds up gradient descent
Strong convexity bounds the gradient, which keeps the iterates bounded
Strong convexity makes the Hessian singular at $x^*$
quiz.e: A convex function can have a flat bottom ($f=0$ on an interval) or no minimiser ($e^x$). The $\frac m2\|y-x\|^2$ floor forces growth away from any point, which gives existence, and strict curvature, which gives uniqueness. Bounding the gradient is smoothness, and the Hessian is at least $mI\succ0$, not singular.

quiz.q: $f$ is 2-strongly convex. At a point $x$, $f(x)=10$ and $\|\nabla f(x)\|=4$. What lower bound does strong convexity give on $z^*=\min f$?
quiz.e: Minimise the lower bound over $y$: $z^*\ge f(x)-\frac1{2m}\|\nabla f(x)\|^2=10-\frac{16}{4}=6$. Using $\frac1m$ instead of $\frac1{2m}$ gives 2; forgetting to square the gradient gives 9.

quiz.q: Under $m$-strong convexity, $f(x)-z^*\le\frac1{2m}\|\nabla f(x)\|^2$. What is the intuition?
o: A bowl with curvature at least $m$ cannot be nearly flat far from its bottom, so a small slope proves you are close to optimal
Smoothness keeps the gradient small near the optimum
The same bound holds for every convex function
Near $x^*$ the function is approximately linear
quiz.e: This is the lecture's step 2: the gradient becomes a certificate of the optimality gap. For a merely convex $f$ it fails: $f(x)=x^4$ near 0 has gap $x^4$ but squared slope $16x^6$, so the ratio $1/(16x^2)$ blows up and no $m$ works, because $x^4$ is too flat at the bottom. Smoothness gives the reverse inequality, $\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\le2M(f(x)-z^*)$.

quiz.q: Ridge regression $f(\beta)=\frac12\|y-X\beta\|^2+\frac\lambda2\|\beta\|^2$ with more features than observations, so $X^\top X$ is singular. Is $f$ strongly convex?
o: Yes: $\nabla^2f=X^\top X+\lambda I\succeq\lambda I$, so $f$ is $m$-strongly convex with $m\ge\lambda$
No: a singular $X^\top X$ means the least-squares term is flat in some direction, so $f$ is only convex
Only if $\lambda$ exceeds the largest eigenvalue of $X^\top X$
Yes, because $X^\top X$ is always positive definite
quiz.e: Least squares alone is flat along the null space of $X$, which is why it has infinitely many minimisers when $p>n$. The penalty adds curvature $\lambda$ in every direction, which restores a unique minimiser and linear GD convergence. Its smoothness constant is $M=\lambda_{\max}(X^\top X)+\lambda$.

quiz.q: Why does gradient descent's linear rate depend on the ratio $M/m$, not on $M$ or $m$ alone?
o: Scaling $f$ by $c>0$ multiplies both $M$ and $m$ by $c$ without changing the problem; only the ratio measures how stretched the level sets are
A larger $M$ always means faster convergence, whatever $m$ is
Only $m$ matters; $M$ enters only the step size
The ratio matters only for non-convex functions
quiz.e: The contraction factor $1-m/M$ is scale-free, as it should be: $f$ and $10f$ have the same minimiser and the same GD path (with $\alpha=1/M$). $M/m$ bounds the condition number of the Hessian, the elongation of the level sets, which is what actually slows GD.

quiz.q: $f$ is $M$-smooth and $m$-strongly convex with $M/m=100$, and GD uses $\alpha=1/M$. About how many iterations does the bound $(1-m/M)^k$ need to shrink $f(x^0)-z^*$ by a factor of $10^6$?
o: About 1,380
About 140
About 14
About 13,800
quiz.e: Need $(0.99)^k\le10^{-6}$, so $k\ge\ln(10^6)/(-\ln0.99)\approx13.8/0.01005\approx1{,}375$, matching $O\big(\frac Mm\log\frac1\varepsilon\big)\approx100\times13.8$. Each factor of 10 in accuracy costs only about 230 more iterations (linear convergence), but each factor of 10 in $M/m$ multiplies the count by 10.

quiz.q: What does a large $M/m$ look like, and why does it slow gradient descent?
o: A long narrow valley: the step must stay at or below $1/M$ to be stable in the steep direction, so along the flat direction (curvature $m$) each step makes only about $m/M$ of the possible progress
A round bowl, where GD overshoots the minimum in every direction
A landscape with many local minima that trap GD
A valley floor where the gradient is exactly zero
quiz.e: Level sets become elongated ellipses. The steep walls force a small step; the gentle floor then needs many small steps, and the iterates zigzag across the valley. Rescaling (diagonal scaling, p.51) reshapes the valley toward a round bowl and fixes this.

quiz.q: Can a function be $m$-strongly convex and $M$-smooth with $m>M$?
o: No: the lower parabola must sit under the upper one, so $m\le M$; when $m=M$, $f$ is a round quadratic and GD with $\alpha=1/M$ reaches $x^*$ in one step
Yes, when $f$ is very strongly convex
Yes, but then gradient descent diverges
No, because a strongly convex function is never smooth
quiz.e: Both bounds hold at the same $x$ and $y$, so $f(x)+\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)+\frac m2\|y-x\|^2\le f(x)+\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)+\frac M2\|y-x\|^2$, which forces $m\le M$. At $m=M$, $f=\frac M2\|x-x^*\|^2+z^*$ and $x^1=x^0-\frac1M M(x^0-x^*)=x^*$, matching the rate factor $1-m/M=0$.

written.q: Let $f(x)=\frac12x_1^2+x_1x_2+2x_2^2-4x_1-4x_2-x_2^3$. (a) Compute $\nabla f$ and $\nabla^2f$. (b) Find all stationary points. (c) Classify each with second-order conditions. (d) Is $f$ convex, and does it have a global minimum? What does this say about relying on gradient descent here?
written.m: (a) $\nabla f=(x_1+x_2-4,\;x_1+4x_2-4-3x_2^2)^\top$, $\nabla^2f=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&4-6x_2\end{pmatrix}$. (b) First component gives $x_1=4-x_2$; substituting, $3x_2-3x_2^2=0$, so $x_2\in\{0,1\}$: points $(4,0)$ and $(3,1)$. (c) At $(4,0)$ the Hessian $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&4\end{pmatrix}$ has leading minors $1>0$ and $3>0$, so it is PD and $(4,0)$ is a strict local minimum. At $(3,1)$ it is $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $-3$, indefinite, so not a local minimum. (d) Not convex: the Hessian is not PSD everywhere (e.g. at $x_2=1$). Along $x=(4,t)$, $f=2t^2-8-t^3\to-\infty$, so there is no global minimum and $(4,0)$ is only local. GD converges to a stationary point that depends on the start; it can reach $(4,0)$ from good starts or diverge from others, and nothing certifies global optimality.
k: Correct gradient and Hessian
Both stationary points found
$(4,0)$ PD so local min; $(3,1)$ indefinite so not a min
Not convex: Hessian not PSD everywhere
Unbounded below, so local is not global
GD only finds stationary points and depends on initialization

written.q: You minimize $f(x)=500x_1^2+20x_1x_2+0.5x_2^2$ with gradient descent. (a) Write $f=\frac12x^\top Qx$, identify $M$ and $m$, and state the linear rate guaranteed with $\alpha=1/M$. (b) Use the condition number to explain why plain GD is slow, and show how diagonal scaling with $D=\mathrm{diag}(1/1000,1)$ helps. (c) Compare exact and backtracking line search as step-size rules for this problem.
written.m: (a) $Q=\begin{pmatrix}1000&20\\20&1\end{pmatrix}$, constant Hessian. $M=\lambda_{\max}\approx1000.4$, $m=\lambda_{\min}\approx0.6$, so $f$ is $M$-smooth and $m$-strongly convex and $f(x^k)-z^*\le(1-m/M)^k(f(x^0)-z^*)$ with $1-m/M\approx1-1/1668$, a very weak contraction. (b) $\kappa(Q)\approx1{,}668$; the Kantorovich factor with exact line search is $((\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1))^2\approx0.998$ per step, and the iterates zig-zag across a long, narrow valley. Scaled GD $x^{k+1}=x^k-\alpha D\nabla f(x^k)$ is GD on $g(y)=f(Sy)$ with $SS^\top=D$; the scaled matrix $D^{1/2}QD^{1/2}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.63\\0.63&1\end{pmatrix}$ has $\kappa\approx4.4$, factor $\approx0.40$. The lecture reports 68 iterations falling to 20. (c) Exact line search picks $\alpha_k\in\arg\min_{\alpha\ge0}f(x^k+\alpha d^k)$: best progress per direction and fewer iterations, but a 1-D optimization each step (closed form for a quadratic). Backtracking shrinks $\alpha$ by $\beta$ until the Armijo condition $f(x^k+\alpha d^k)\le f(x^k)+\sigma\alpha\nabla f(x^k)^\top d^k$ holds: cheaper per step, more iterations.
k: Correct $Q$ with off-diagonal 20
$M$, $m$ as extreme eigenvalues; rate $1-m/M$
$\kappa\approx1668$ and the Kantorovich factor
Scaled update and equivalence to GD on $f(Sy)$
Scaled $\kappa\approx4.4$, 68 to 20 iterations
Exact vs backtracking: work per iteration vs number of iterations

written.q: Let $f$ be $M$-smooth and $m$-strongly convex, and run gradient descent with $\alpha=1/M$. (a) Use the smoothness bound to show $f(x^{k+1})\le f(x^k)-\frac1{2M}\|\nabla f(x^k)\|^2$. (b) Use the strong-convexity bound to show $z^*\ge f(x^k)-\frac1{2m}\|\nabla f(x^k)\|^2$. (c) Combine them into $f(x^{k+1})-z^*\le(1-\frac mM)(f(x^k)-z^*)$. (d) In one or two sentences each, explain what (a) and (b) mean intuitively, and why the rate depends only on $M/m$.
written.m:
(a) Put $y=x^{k+1}=x^k- rac1M
abla f(x^k)$ in $f(y)\le f(x)+
abla f(x)^	op(y-x)+ rac M2\|y-x\|^2$: $f(x^{k+1})\le f(x^k)- rac1M\|
abla f\|^2+ rac1{2M}\|
abla f\|^2=f(x^k)- rac1{2M}\|
abla f(x^k)\|^2$.
(b) The right side of $f(y)\ge f(x^k)+
abla f(x^k)^	op(y-x^k)+ rac m2\|y-x^k\|^2$ is minimised at $y=x^k- rac1m
abla f(x^k)$, with value $f(x^k)- rac1{2m}\|
abla f(x^k)\|^2$. Since $f(y)$ is at least that for every $y$, so is $z^*$.
(c) From (b), $\|
abla f(x^k)\|^2\ge2m(f(x^k)-z^*)$. Substitute into (a) and subtract $z^*$: $f(x^{k+1})-z^*\le f(x^k)-z^*- rac mM(f(x^k)-z^*)$.
(d) (a): the ceiling guarantees progress proportional to the squared slope; a step of $1/M$ can never overshoot. (b): the floor means a gentle slope only happens near the bottom, so the slope measures how far from optimal you are. The rate is $1-m/M$: scaling $f$ scales $M$ and $m$ together, so only their ratio, the conditioning, matters.
k: Correct substitution of $\alpha=1/M$ into the smoothness bound
Minimises the strong-convexity lower bound over $y$
Combines into the $(1-m/M)$ contraction
Ceiling intuition: guaranteed decrease, a safe step
Floor intuition: the gradient certifies the gap
Rate is scale-free and depends on $M/m$

written.q: Let $f(x)=\frac12(x_1^2+\kappa x_2^2)$ with $\kappa\ge1$. (a) Find the smallest $M$ and largest $m$. (b) Run one step of gradient descent with $\alpha=1/M$ from $x^0=(1,1)$ and give $x^1$. (c) How fast does each coordinate converge, and what happens when $\kappa=1000$? (d) Explain the result geometrically.
written.m:
(a) $\nabla^2f=\mathrm{diag}(1,\kappa)$, so $M=\kappa$, $m=1$, $M/m=\kappa$.
(b) $\nabla f(x)=(x_1,\kappa x_2)$, so $x^1=(1-\frac1\kappa,\;1-1)=(1-\frac1\kappa,\,0)$.
(c) The steep coordinate $x_2$ is solved in one step; the flat coordinate shrinks by the factor $1-1/\kappa$ each step. At $\kappa=1000$ that is $0.999$ per step: about 6,900 steps to reduce $x_1$ by $10^3$, matching $O(\frac Mm\log\frac1\varepsilon)$.
(d) The level sets are ellipses stretched $\sqrt\kappa$ times longer along $x_1$. The step has to be short enough for the steep $x_2$ walls ($\alpha\le1/M$, or $<2/M$ to avoid divergence), which makes it tiny relative to the gentle $x_1$ slope. A diagonal rescaling $x_2\to x_2/\sqrt\kappa$ would make the bowl round and GD would finish in one step.
k: $M=\kappa$, $m=1$
Correct $x^1=(1-1/\kappa,0)$
Per-coordinate rates: one step vs factor $1-1/\kappa$
Iteration count of order $\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon)$
Narrow-valley picture: the step is limited by the steep direction
Mentions scaling as the fix
